title: Jump Game VIII
statement:
You start at index 0 of an integer array `nums` of length `n` and want to end at index `n - 1`. Jumps only go forward: from index `i` you may land on an index `j > i` when one of these holds:

- `nums[j] >= nums[i]`, and every value strictly between the two positions (indices `k` with `i < k < j`) is **less than** `nums[i]`;
- `nums[j] < nums[i]`, and every value strictly between the two positions is **greater than or equal to** `nums[i]`.

When there is nothing between `i` and `j`, the condition on the values between holds automatically. Landing on index `j` costs `costs[j]` (the starting index 0 is never paid for). Return the smallest total cost of a sequence of jumps from index 0 to index `n - 1` (0 when `n == 1`).
notes:
## Intuition

The rules leave each index `i` with at most two possible jumps. The first kind must land on a value `>= nums[i]` with only smaller values in between, so it can only be the **first** later index whose value is `>= nums[i]`. The second kind must land on a value `< nums[i]` with only values `>= nums[i]` in between, so it can only be the first later index whose value is `< nums[i]`. All jumps go forward, so a left-to-right DP over these at most `2n` edges finds the cheapest route. Checking every pair `i < j` against the rule also works but costs O(n²) or worse.

Two monotonic stacks find both "first later index" targets in one pass: an index waits on a stack until the element that ends its wait arrives, and that element is exactly its jump target.

## Approach

1. `dp[j]` is the cheapest cost to stand on index `j`; `dp[0] = 0`, the rest start at `Infinity`.
2. Scan `j` from left to right.
3. While the top of `waitingForHigher` has a value `<= nums[j]`, pop it as `i`: `j` is its first later index with a value at least as big, so relax `dp[j]` with `dp[i] + costs[j]`.
4. While the top of `waitingForLower` has a value `> nums[j]`, pop it as `i`: `j` is its first later smaller value, so relax `dp[j]` the same way.
5. Push `j` on both stacks and continue. Return `dp[n - 1]`.

Every edge into `j` comes from an earlier index, so `dp[i]` is final whenever it is used.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3,2,4,4,1]`, `costs = [3,7,6,4,2]`.

- `j = 1` (value 2): index 0 (value 3) leaves `waitingForLower`, `dp[1] = 0 + 7 = 7`.
- `j = 2` (value 4): indices 1 and 0 leave `waitingForHigher`, `dp[2] = min(7 + 6, 0 + 6) = 6`.
- `j = 3` (value 4): index 2 leaves `waitingForHigher` (equal values count), `dp[3] = 6 + 4 = 10`.
- `j = 4` (value 1): indices 3, 2, 1 leave `waitingForLower`, `dp[4] = min(10 + 2, 6 + 2, 7 + 2) = 8`.

The answer is `8`: jump 0 → 2 → 4.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each index is pushed and popped at most once per stack.
- Space: O(n) for `dp` and the stacks.

## Pitfalls

- Equal values: a later equal value is a valid "higher" target, so pop on `<=`, while the "lower" stack pops only on a strictly smaller value (`>`).
- The cost belongs to the landing index; index 0 is never charged.
- Totals can reach about 10^10, beyond 32-bit integers: use `long` in Java and C.
- Every `i` can always jump to `i + 1` (nothing lies between), so `dp[n - 1]` is never `Infinity`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `dp` | cheapest total cost to reach each index |
| `waitingForHigher` | indices still waiting for a later value `>=` theirs (values strictly decreasing) |
| `waitingForLower` | indices still waiting for a later value `<` theirs (values non-decreasing) |
| `j` | the index being reached |
| `i` | an index whose jump lands on `j` |

narration.3: Every index starts unreachable at infinite cost.
narration.4: We stand on index 0 for free.
narration.5: Indices whose first later value at least as big has not appeared yet.
narration.6: Indices whose first later strictly smaller value has not appeared yet.
narration.7: Scan the array; j is the index being landed on.
narration.8: nums[j] is at least the top's value, and everything above it was smaller, so j is the top's first-kind jump.
narration.9: Take that index i off the stack; its wait is over.
narration.10: Reaching j from i costs dp[i] plus the price of landing on j.
narration.12: nums[j] is strictly below the top's value, and everything in between was at least as big, so j is its second-kind jump.
narration.13: Take that index i off the stack.
narration.14: Relax dp[j] with the jump from i.
narration.16: j now waits for its own first later value that is at least as big...
narration.17: ...and for its first later value that is smaller.
narration.19: The cheapest cost to land on the last index.
